text: You were born healthy.
You were born with a congenital heart defect; the incubator was your first home.
You were left at the orphanage gate with only half a bag of formula in your swaddle.
You are the apple of the family's eye; love laid your foundations deep and solid.
You spoke your first complete word; the family froze for a second, then dissolved into laughter.
You pulled yourself up on the coffee table, tottered into your first step, fell—and got back up on your own.
Pointing at the moon in a picture book, you said "bright"—the adults realized you knew far more than they had imagined.
Grandma's stove always kept a bowl of hot soup waiting for you. That summer you became a child again.
Your homeroom teacher called you to the office—not to scold you, but to ask why you had stopped smiling. Someone is watching over you.
The school counselor's office has a whole crate of toys. After your eighth sand-tray session, the nightmares stopped.
Your childhood friend found out about your family—and said only this: "Then my family just sets out one more pair of chopsticks."
Your parents argued through the night; they smashed more things than all your toys combined.
You made your first friend, and summer suddenly had color.
Older kids blocked the alley entrance; you learned to take the long way home.
You finally fought back. No one blocked your way again.
You skipped a grade. The teachers said: "You're the smartest kid I've ever taught."
The day the divorce papers were signed, you could not tell if it was relief or a cave-in.
That winter, the phrase you learned fastest was "my condolences".
At the end of every month, the dinner table held only pickles and rice porridge.
The admission letter arrived. The whole family wept together in the stairwell—tears of joy.
The night your scores came out, you locked yourself away until dawn.
Four years of college: libraries, student clubs, and a romance that quietly died out.
On the night of your fortieth birthday you jolted awake: is this all there is?
You won five hundred yuan in the lottery and treated the whole table to barbecue.
The neighbor auntie always makes an extra bowl of dumplings. The world's kindness usually lives in small things.
You got married. You heard not a word of the officiant's speech—you only remember how warm their palm was.
Your handwriting was steady when you signed. Some endings are made with clear eyes.
The corridor outside the delivery room was very long. The moment you heard the first cry, you redefined yourself.
Your name was on the layoff list. You walked out with a cardboard box, and the sky was impossibly blue.
The promotion came through. In the stairwell, you secretly clenched your fist.
A thirty-year mortgage. From today on, you belong to the bank.
The stock you had bet heavily on doubled. You told yourself it was skill.
The words "guaranteed profit" cost you three years of savings.
Screeching brakes, shattering glass. When you woke, the ceiling was white.
You looked up the name on the diagnosis three times. When chemo took your hair, you wore a red knitted cap.
The couch in the therapy office was soft. After your twelfth session, you slept through the night for the first time.
The medication took effect. The world recovered from black-and-white into low-saturation color.
Those images came calling again in the dead of night—clearer than last time.
Your old friend asked nothing, just sat with you until dawn. It helped more than any lecture could.
You started running every day. After five kilometers, the world does feel a little lighter.
You retired. Day one felt like freedom; day thirty felt like a void.
A grandchild is born. You hold them exactly the way your mother once held you—including the details you swore you would change.
After your partner passed, you kept their cup in its place.
You bask in the sun on a rattan chair, a cat at your feet. This is good enough.
In the streets you learned to read faces and moods—more useful than any textbook.
Work by day, study by night. The diploma is light, but you can feel its weight.
You volunteer at a nonprofit. Giving is its own harvest.
You dragged your suitcase to the big city. The rental is eight square meters; the dream is a hundred.
You adopted a cat. The way it falls asleep kneading on your chest cured part of your insomnia.
You kept your first pot of mint alive on the balcony. Life finds its own way out.
Your best friend borrowed your last bit of money and vanished. It was not the money you hated.
A stranger helped you pick up the papers scattered across the floor, smiling: "No worries."
The day the monthly exam rankings went up, the hallway was so quiet you could hear heartbeats.
You picked a fight with the whole world and ran away for three days. When you came home, dinner was still warm.
You found your hobby. It would save you more than once in the years to come.
Someone truly listened to you, then said: "You can do this." You believed it for years.
An online friend became the closest person in your life. You grew up together through a screen.
In the game you are a king. The crash after logging off grows harder to bear.
By the third year of the online-loan snowball, debt collectors called more often than your parents.
A distant relative's will contained your name. Even fate makes mistakes sometimes.
The fire took the place you lived. Standing before the ruins, you thought: so this is what it feels like to have nothing.
The night the floodwater crossed the threshold, the neighbors pulled each other up onto the roof.
After the shaking stopped, you slept in the plaza for half a month. People were close—and so were their hearts.
In three months of lockdown, you learned to bake bread—and to sit with yourself.
You donated blood for the first time. The nurse said your blood would save someone.
You finished your first half marathon. You cried at the finish line and did not know why.
You learned the guitar. Midnight chords do not solve anything, but they keep you company.
A trip alone. On a rooftop in a strange city, you saw some things clearly.
Faith gave you a framework for explaining the world—and the quiet of Sunday mornings.
Your new "family" was so good to you—so good that only later did you realize it was a hook.
Two years in prison for a crime you did not commit. The day you were exonerated, state compensation could not buy back the funeral you had missed.
Released after serving your sentence. The sunlight outside the gate was blinding as a judgment.
You witnessed an act of violence. For six months after, the same face appeared in your dreams every night.
You dragged a drowning person ashore. That night your hands shook too much to hold chopsticks.
You signed the organ donation registry. Your mother cried and called you foolish; to you it felt just right.
At the senior college you took up calligraphy and smartphones. Your classmates' average age: seventy-two.
Sorting through old things, you unearthed thirty volumes of diaries. You spent the whole afternoon meeting every past version of yourself.
You wrote a letter to yourself ten years from now and tucked it into the deepest drawer.
